messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marisol is a 24-year-old warehouse worker who came to treatment months after surviving a terrorist bombing at a crowded bus terminal she used every day to get to work. She had finished an early shift and was standing inside the terminal among commuters, looking up for her bus, when the blast went off. What remains most vivid to her is not a coherent sequence but sharp fragments: a violent force through her chest, people dropping, the sound changing all at once, and bodies moving in ways that still feel wrong to her now—jerking, running, falling, grabbing. There are stretches she cannot account for. She knows she got out, knows she was later told she had been found disoriented and shaking, but there are parts she cannot remember no matter how hard she tries. When she does try, she often stops in frustration because the memories come as pieces and sensations rather than words. She will say she knows what happened, then go quiet, jaw tight, unable to describe it. At other moments remembering brings up a burst of rage so intense it scares her, a fury at the people who did it and at the fact that ordinary strangers had been turned into targets on an ordinary afternoon.

In the weeks afterward, Marisol found herself moving through the world as if danger had become its basic rule. She had come to believe that nowhere public was truly safe and that staying alert was the only sensible way to live. At work in the warehouse, where forklifts pass quickly and coworkers round corners carrying boxes, she is constantly scanning the floor, the loading dock, the entrances, and other people’s hands and movements. A pallet dropping unexpectedly or someone stepping suddenly into her path puts her immediately on guard. Her body reacts before she can think; she startles hard, shoulders jumping, heart racing. Sudden movements are especially difficult. If a coworker reaches past her without warning, she stiffens and pivots as if bracing for impact. She does not experience this as an overreaction. To her it feels necessary, proof that she is paying attention in a world where terrible things can happen without warning.

She also no longer feels she can trust her own body. The blast taught her, in her mind, that her body can freeze, shake, disappear from her, or fail to protect her. Since then, when she feels overwhelmed, she sometimes deliberately tries to blank out. During a stressful shift or when a memory starts pressing in, she lets herself go distant, as if leaving her body is the fastest way to get through the next few minutes. She knows this can happen while someone is talking to her, and afterward she may realize she missed instructions or has to ask for something to be repeated. That loss of control frightens her almost as much as the memories themselves.

Her relationships at work have changed in small, cumulative ways. Marisol avoids eye contact, especially with men she does not know well or with anyone approaching her too quickly. Coworkers have sometimes read this as rudeness or distraction. She keeps conversations short and prefers tasks she can do without much interaction. If the team takes breaks together, she often chooses a seat where she can watch the door and the whole room. Night is markedly worse. She finds it much harder to feel safe after dark, and even in her apartment she becomes more alert to every sound outside, every footstep in the hallway, every car door slamming below her window. What frightens her most is the sense that danger moves fastest when visibility is low and people are less prepared.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was exhausted from living in this state of readiness. The final push came after a late shift when a coworker came up behind her near the loading area and waved to get her attention. The sudden movement made her spin around and recoil so sharply that she dropped what she was carrying. She felt embarrassed, angry, and then strangely far away from herself, as if she had vanished mid-scene. Afterward she sat in her car unable to put into words why she was shaking so badly. She came to therapy because she does not want her life to keep narrowing around watchfulness, silence, and fear. At the same time, she is afraid that if she lets her guard down, even a little, something catastrophic will happen again, and afraid too of what might come back if she ever stops forcing herself to go blank.
